The ''' 1941 [[German football championship]]''', the 34th edition of the competition, was won by [[SK Rapid Wien]], the club's sole German championship. Rapid, which had previously won twelve [[List of Austrian football champions|Austrian football championship]]s between 1911 and 1938 as well as the [[1938 Tschammerpokal|1938 German Cup]], won the competition by defeating [[FC Schalke 04|Schalke 04]] 4–3 in the final.<ref name="List" >[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesd/duitchamp.html (West) Germany -List of champions] rsssf.org, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref><ref>[http://www.weltfussball.de/teams/fc-schalke-04/1/ FC Schalke 04 » Steckbrief] {{in lang|de}} Weltfussball.de – FC Schalke 04 honours, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref><ref>[http://www.weltfussball.de/teams/rapid-wien/1/ Rapid Wien » Steckbrief] {{in lang|de}} Weltfussball.de – Rapid Wien honours, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref> The final was held on 22 June 1941, the same day [[Nazi Germany]] invaded the [[Soviet Union]] in [[Operation Barbarossa]].<ref>[https://www.welt.de/kultur/history/article13444013/Der-laengste-Tag-das-Protokoll-des-Ueberfalls.html Der längste Tag – das Protokoll des Überfalls] ''[[Die Welt]]'', published: 22 June 2011, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref>

==Overview==
[[File:Bundesarchiv Bild 183-2004-1001-503, Berlin, Zuschauer beim Fußball-Endspiel.jpg|200px|thumb|right|The score board of the 1941 final]]
FC Schalke 04, having won five of the previous seven finals, being the defending champions and aiming for an unprecedented third consecutive German championship, were the favourites and led the final 3–0 after 57 minutes but Rapid scored four unanswered goals, the last three of them by [[Franz Binder]], to win the championship.<ref>[http://www.weltfussball.de/spielbericht/deutsche-meisterschaft-1941-finale-rapid-wien-fc-schalke-04/ Deutsche Meisterschaft 1940/1941 » Finale » Rapid Wien – FC Schalke 04 4:3] {{in lang|de}} Weltfussball.de, Game report, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref> It marked the second of three occasions of a club from [[Vienna]] (German: ''Wien'') in the final, Rapid becoming the only one to win the competition while [[Admira Wien]] had made a losing appearance in the [[1939 German football championship|1939]] final and [[First Vienna FC]] would do the same in [[1942 German football championship|1942]].<ref name="List" /> Austrian clubs had  played in the German league system from 1938, after the ''[[Anschluss]]'', until the [[German Instrument of Surrender|German surrender]] in 1945.<ref>[http://www.sportal.de/die-deutsche-vergangenheit-von-rapid-wien-1-2012102523664400000 Die deutsche Vergangenheit von Rapid Wien] {{in lang|de}} sportal.de, The German history of Rapid Wien, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref>

Rapid's victory led to a number of conspiracy theories. On Schalke's side it was speculated that Rapid was allowed to win to award a national championship to a club from the ''[[Ostmark (Austria)|Ostmark]]'' while, in Austria, the theory developed that Rapid players were punished after the final by being sent to the [[front line]]. Both theories were disproven when Rapid, in 2009, commissioned a study into the history of the club during the Nazi era and found no evidence for either.<ref>[http://kurier.at/sport/fussball/deutscher-meister-rapid-1-leverkusen-0/825.084 Deutscher Meister: Rapid 1, Leverkusen 0] {{in lang|de}} ''[[Kurier]]'', published: 25 December 2012, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref> Rapid continues to list both German titles, the 1941 championship and the 1938 cup win, in its honours.<ref>[http://www.skrapid.at/de/startseite/verein/der-sk-rapid/erfolge/ Erfolge] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160109004947/http://www.skrapid.at/de/startseite/verein/der-sk-rapid/erfolge/ |date=9 January 2016 }} {{in lang|de}} Rapid Wien website – honours, accessed: 27 December 2015</ref>

Schalke's [[Hermann Eppenhoff]] became the top scorer of the 1941 championship with 15 goals, the highest individual amount for any player in the history of the competition from 1903 to 1963.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weltfussball.de/torschuetzenkoenige/deutsche-meisterschaft/ |title=Deutsche Meisterschaft » Torschützenkönige |website= Weltfussball.de |access-date= 2 January 2016|language=de|trans-title=German championship: Top goal scorer}}</ref>

The twenty [[1940–41 Gauliga|1940–41]] [[Gauliga]] champions, two more than in [[1940 German football championship|1940]] because of the addition of the [[Gauliga Elsaß]] and [[Gauliga Danzig-Westpreußen]],<ref name="ReferenceA">''kicker Allmanach 1990'', page: 243-245</ref> competed in a group stage with the four group winners advancing to the semi-finals. The two semi-final winners then contested the 1941 championship final. The groups were divided into two with four clubs and two with six clubs with the latter, in turn, subdivided into two groups of three teams each and a final of these group winners to determine the overall group champions.<ref name="Rsssf" >[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesd/duithistpre45.html German championship 1941] rsssf.org, accessed: 26 December 2015</ref>

In the following season, the German championship was played with twenty five clubs. From there it gradually expanded further through a combination of territorial expansion of [[Nazi Germany]] and the sub-dividing of the Gauligas in later years, reaching a strength of thirty-one in its last completed season, 1943–44.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>
